title: August and the Portrait
premise: Folklorist Odile Vasquez has spent three years in the village of Hollowmere recording songs no one will sing twice, telling herself the nocturnal counting sounds are wind, pipes, or owls. When an excavation crew unearths a door sealed from the inside beneath the old Vasquez estate, Odile learns the village's founding family bound something below that counts the living each August, and this year it has begun counting early. To save the descendants—including the reluctant heir Tomas and his daughter—Odile must finish the song cycle that keeps the seal intact, even though completing it demands she give the thing below her own name and voice. In the end, Odile sings herself into the count, buying the family a generation, while Tomas carries her recordings out of Hollowmere so someone will remember what was paid.
about_author: Marguerite Kavanagh is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing oral histories in remote farming communities before turning to fiction. She writes horror rooted in folk tradition, where the oldest songs are contracts and every inheritance comes with terms.

chapters.title: The Songs They Won't Repeat
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. She records an elderly singer who performs a lullaby once, then refuses, hands shaking, saying 'the second time invites.' That night Odile hears rhythmic knocking beneath her rented room and logs it as settling pipes. Emotional beat: professional curiosity masking three years of quiet dread.

chapters.title: Hollowmere's Polite Silence
chapters.summary: Odile interviews villagers for context; each conversation curdles when she mentions the Vasquez estate or the month of August. The pub empties around her. Her landlady leaves salt on her windowsill without explanation. POV: Odile. Emotional beat: isolation sharpening into the sense that everyone knows something they've agreed not to say.

chapters.title: The Excavation
chapters.summary: A heritage crew begins surveying the collapsed east wing of the Vasquez estate. Odile watches from the fence line, recognizing the site from a fragmentary ballad about a door 'shut from within.' The foreman jokes about bad air down there. POV: Odile. Emotional beat: dread arriving ahead of evidence.

chapters.title: Sealed From the Inside
chapters.summary: The crew unearths a stone door whose bolt mechanism sits on the buried side. Work stops by unanimous, unspoken consent. Odile photographs it and finds her own reflection in the image looks wrong—mouth open mid-word. POV: Odile. Emotional beat: the moment explanation fails.

chapters.title: Tomas Comes Down the Hill
chapters.summary: Tomas Vasquez, estranged heir selling the estate, arrives with his daughter Wren and orders the dig filled in. He coldly rebuffs Odile's questions, but she notices he flinches at the evening knocking too. POV: Tomas. Emotional beat: a man performing indifference over inherited terror.

chapters.title: Wren Counts to Forty
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. His daughter begins sleep-talking numbers, ascending nightly: thirty-one, thirty-two, thirty-three. A pediatrician finds nothing wrong. Tomas checks the estate cellar and finds fresh scratches inside a sealed hatch. Emotional beat: paternal helplessness curdling into certainty.

chapters.title: What the Archive Wouldn't Keep
chapters.summary: Odile travels to a county records office and finds the Vasquez founding deed torn out, but a marginal note survives: 'the tithe of names, renewed each August.' The archivist who helps her later doesn't answer her calls. POV: Odile. Emotional beat: scholarship becoming complicity.

chapters.title: The First Missing
chapters.summary: A excavation worker vanishes; his truck remains, doors locked from inside. The village holds no search. At the vigil, no one speaks above a whisper after dark. POV: Odile. Emotional beat: grief the community refuses to perform, because mourning is a kind of naming.

chapters.title: Terms of Inheritance
chapters.summary: Tomas discovers his grandfather's ledger: generations of Vasquez names entered each August, the list shortening as the family thins. This year's page is blank except for two entries already inked in a hand like wet clay: WREN, TOMAS. POV: Tomas. Emotional beat: duty revealed as predation.

chapters.title: The Song Cycle
chapters.summary: Odile assembles her three years of recordings and realizes the refused second verses form one continuous song—a binding, sung in halves by different villagers so no one bears it whole. Completing it requires a singer willing to be named in it. POV: Odile. Emotional beat: purpose crystallizing into terrible clarity.

chapters.title: Love Against Duty
chapters.summary: Odile and Tomas, allies now, grow close over late nights transcribing verses. He begs her to leave with Wren before August ends; she refuses to abandon the village. Their first kiss happens under the knocking. POV: alternating. Emotional beat: tenderness discovered at the worst possible hour.

chapters.title: The Count Reaches Thirty-Nine
chapters.summary: Wren's sleep-counting hits thirty-nine—the number of souls in Hollowmere. Odile cross-checks: forty residents last spring. The thing below isn't predicting; it's tallying as it takes. POV: Odile. Emotional beat: arithmetic as horror.

chapters.title: Villagers of the Second Verse
chapters.summary: Odile confronts the elderly singers, and one finally explains: their ancestors split the binding song so the burden would be shared and deniable. Singing it whole means offering yourself as the anchor. The old woman agrees to teach Odile anyway. POV: Odile. Emotional beat: gratitude and fury braided together.

chapters.title: Salt on Every Sill
chapters.summary: The village attempts collective protection—salt, iron, silence after dusk—but the knocking moves house to house, learning. A child goes missing. The vicar burns his own records rather than let Odile copy them. POV: Tomas. Emotional beat: a community's defenses failing one superstition at a time.

chapters.title: The Door Opens Inward
chapters.summary: The excavated door is found ajar despite being guarded; cold air breathes out, smelling of turned earth and old hymns. Inside, walls are scored with thousands of tally marks—and one fresh set, still wet. POV: Odile. Emotional beat: the boundary between above and below formally abolished.

chapters.title: Wren's Bargain
chapters.summary: Ten-year-old Wren reveals she's been speaking with 'the lady under the floor,' who only wants to be sung to properly. Wren offers to go instead of her father. Tomas, shattered, locks her window; the count reaches Wren's name anyway. POV: Tomas. Emotional beat: a parent discovering he cannot stand between his child and the debt.

chapters.title: The Last Verse Learned
chapters.summary: On the final night of August, Odile masters the complete song in the church, the old woman conducting with trembling hands. The melody requires the singer's true name woven into the final line—an anchor, freely given. POV: Odile. Emotional beat: resolve hardening into sacrifice.

chapters.title: August Ends Early
chapters.summary: The climax. At the opened door, Odile sings the full cycle as the thing below rises through the tally-marked dark, wearing the voices of the taken. Tomas holds the light; Wren adds the child's descant her grandmother taught her. The final line names Odile, and the door draws her gently down. POV: alternating Odile and Tomas. Emotional beat: love and duty reconciled in a single act of chosen loss.

chapters.title: After the Counting Stops
chapters.summary: Silence falls on Hollowmere for the first time in living memory. The missing are not returned, but the knocking ceases, the salt is swept away, and Wren sleeps without numbers. Tomas cannot remember Odile's face, only her voice on tape. POV: Tomas. Emotional beat: relief shadowed by erasure.

chapters.title: The Recordings
chapters.summary: Tomas plays Odile's tapes and finds one labeled in her handwriting: FOR WHOEVER STAYS. On it, she explains what she did and asks him to keep the song alive—not as a binding, but as a memory. Wren listens beside him, mouthing the words she somehow already knows. POV: Tomas. Emotional beat: grief transformed into stewardship.

chapters.title: Inheritance, Revised
chapters.summary: Tomas withdraws the estate from sale and establishes it as an archive for Odile's fieldwork, hiring the surviving singers to document the complete cycle lawfully, openly, together. The village, slowly, learns to sing the second verse aloud. POV: Tomas. Emotional beat: justice built outside any court, from testimony and care.

chapters.title: Someone Will Remember What Was Paid
chapters.summary: Epilogue, one year later. Wren, now the archive's youngest volunteer, records the full song for the first time—and in the final line, faintly, a second voice joins hers from somewhere beneath the floorboards, singing her name back, kindly, like a lullaby. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: peace with a pulse; the horror endures, but so does the love.
